The tree edges are numbered in the accent color in discovery order: 1 A-D, 2 A-C, 3 A-B, 4 D-F and 5 C-E. E is reached from C before B, so the edge B-E, drawn dashed, is not in the tree. The card lists the five (parent, child) pairs." width="100%"} The general form of `bfs_edges()`: instead of following a node's edges, the search asks a function `neighbors(node)` which nodes to go to next, and in what order. Use it to search along only some edges (only one edge type, or only edges above a weight, say, without building a subgraph), to visit neighbors in a custom order, or to search over links that are not edges of the graph at all. As in `bfs_edges()`, each newly reached node is discovered along exactly one edge, so the result is a tree. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The starting node, as an integer ID or a string label. [neighbors]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Callable[[int], Any] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A function taking a node ID and returning an iterable of the nodes to visit from it (as IDs or labels), in the order to visit them. It is called once for every node reached, when the node is reached. If `None` (default), each node's out-neighbors in edge insertion order, as `bfs_edges()` follows them. [depth_limit]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Stop expanding at this many hops from the source. If `None` (default), there is no limit. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `(parent, child)` node-ID pairs in the order the children were discovered. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the source or a node `neighbors` supplies does not exist, or `depth_limit=` is negative. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~bfs_edges`) : The same search over the graph's own edges. [](`~generic_edge_bfs`) : The edge counterpart, which visits every edge a callback supplies. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A breadth-first search over the nodes `neighbors` supplies: each node is called for once, when first reached, and its children are queued in the order given. Nodes the callback names twice, or that were already reached, are skipped. The search stops as soon as every node of the graph has been reached. Matches NetworkX's `generic_bfs_edges`, the node counterpart of NetworkX pull request #8950's `generic_edge_bfs`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} By default the search follows the graph's edges, as `bfs_edges()` does: ::: {#229f9eee .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["hub", "a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]) g.add_edges([("hub", "a"), ("hub", "b"), ("hub", "c"), ("b", "d"), ("c", "e")]) label = g.get_label_from_id [(label(p), label(c)) for p, c in g.generic_bfs_edges("hub")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [('hub', 'a'), ('hub', 'b'), ('hub', 'c'), ('b', 'd'), ('c', 'e')] ``` ::: ::: A `neighbors` function can change the order: here each node's neighbors are visited in reverse alphabetical order, so `c` and its child `e` come first: ::: {#a64863f7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def reverse_alphabetical(node): return sorted(g.get_neighbors(node), key=label, reverse=True) [(label(p), label(c)) for p, c in g.generic_bfs_edges("hub", reverse_alphabetical)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [('hub', 'c'), ('hub', 'b'), ('hub', 'a'), ('c', 'e'), ('b', 'd')] ``` ::: :::
